name: Sam Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. I'm going to describe five pictures of how AI might change work and ask how you'd react. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm Sam, 43, and I work on a renovation crew, kitchens, loft conversions, the odd extension. I've been doing it about three years. Before that I worked in a bank branch for fifteen years, until they closed it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Before the pictures, tell me about a normal working day for you. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The firm's family-run, Hale and Sons, six of us on the tools. A normal day, we're in someone's house by eight, I'm ripping out an old kitchen or fitting the joists for a loft floor, and Mr Hale's son Rob is showing me for the third time how to scribe a worktop to a crooked wall. I like that every house is different, and the people make you tea and tell you their life story. What wears me out is the dust, and the feeling that I'm the oldest apprentice in the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, it's always somewhere in between. At the bank they said apps would end branches in two years and it took ten. I'd say that to the lads in the van and they'd tell me to stop talking about banks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means steady. I'd keep learning, Rob would keep correcting me, and in a few years I'd be good. The bank taught me that the future always comes, it just comes slower than the leaflets say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd keep using the AI app now and then to check the building rules for loft stairs, because Rob hates paperwork. Mei and I would keep putting money aside like we do, and maybe I'd start taking on small jobs for neighbours on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the bank closing. How did that go for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I took the redundancy package, which was decent after fifteen years. I sat in the car outside the branch on the last day for about twenty minutes. Then I rang a friend whose brother-in-law was Mr Hale, and that's how I got into this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Mei think of your career change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a pharmacist, she earns more than me and always has, which never bothered either of us. She thought I'd last six months. Three years later she shows people photos of my kitchens on her phone, which is nice.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, since it's always somewhere in between, like apps taking ten years rather than two to close bank branches.
S0.think: He thinks it means steady progress for him, learning the trade over a few years. The bank taught him the future comes slower than the leaflets say.
S0.do: Carries on learning with the renovation crew and uses an AI app now and then to check building rules. Keeps saving with Mei and may start small Saturday jobs for neighbours.
S0.quote: The bank taught me that the future always comes, it just comes slower than the leaflets say.
S0.fieldNote: Sam reads every picture through his fifteen years in a bank branch that closed slowly. He's measured, a little dry, and uses AI only now and then for paperwork. His partner's higher pharmacist wage and his redundancy package make him feel secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like the banks again, the boring tasks go first and people need to adjust. I'd say firms should train people and government should help those who fall through. Nothing dramatic, just sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be mostly fine. Renovating old houses is messy, every wall is crooked, and I don't see a robot scribing a worktop to Mrs Patel's kitchen wall any time soon. The work that's hard for me is exactly the work that's hard for a machine, which is oddly comforting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once Rob or the others started using something and it worked, like an app that measures a room from photos, I'd use it too. I'd do the Saturday jobs for neighbours and use the AI to help price them, because pricing is where I'm weakest. I'd put the extra money in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit alert, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'once Rob started using it'. Why wait for him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because at the bank we had three new systems in five years, and two of them were scrapped. I learned to let someone else find the bugs. Once it's proven, I'm quick enough to pick it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks at the bank went first, back then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Counting cash, paying in cheques, then mortgage appointments went online. The last thing to go was the old people who wanted to talk to a person. I think the same will happen with renovations, the talking bit lasts longest.

S1.say: I'd say it's like the banks again, with boring tasks going first and people needing to adjust. Firms should train people and government should help those who fall through.
S1.think: He thinks he'd mostly be fine because renovating crooked old houses is hard for machines. The work that's hard for him is also hard for a robot.
S1.do: Adopts tools like a photo-measuring app once colleagues have proved them. Takes Saturday jobs for neighbours, uses AI to help price them, and saves the extra money.
S1.feel: Calm, with a bit of alertness.
S1.quote: The work that's hard for me is exactly the work that's hard for a machine, which is oddly comforting.
S1.fieldNote: Sam's lesson from the bank is to let others find the bugs first. He takes comfort that crooked old houses are hard for both him and robots. He predicts the talking part of the work will last longest, as it did in banking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going far too fast and the government needs to slow it down and look after people in the meantime. I'd say companies have a responsibility too. I'd try not to sound hysterical, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think it means my second career ends about as soon as it's started. And Mei's job is half checking prescriptions, which a machine would do. Twice in five years I'd be sat in the car outside a workplace that doesn't need me any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd sit down that week and go through the numbers, like I used to with customers. Cut the extras: the new car, the extension we were planning on our own house. Put more into savings and pay down the mortgage, and rethink whether Oscar takes on a big loan for university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, we've got savings, but the knot would be there every morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you be doing in those two years while you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving every penny I could. I wouldn't retrain, because two years isn't enough to become anything a machine can't already be. I'd mostly be trying to make sure the house is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Oscar about university?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's fifteen and wants to do engineering. I'd say, if it's free or cheap, go, because learning is never wasted. But I wouldn't want him carrying a debt for a job that might not exist by the time he finishes, and that's an awful thing to tell your son.

S2.say: I'd say it's going far too fast, the government must slow it and look after people, and companies carry responsibility too. I'd try not to sound hysterical.
S2.think: He thinks his second career would end almost as soon as it started, and his partner's pharmacy work is exposed too. He pictures himself in a car outside another workplace that doesn't need him.
S2.do: Goes through the household numbers that week and cuts the new car and their own planned extension. Saves more, pays down the mortgage and rethinks Oscar's university loan.
S2.feel: Anxious every morning, but not panicked because of savings.
S2.quote: Twice in five years I'd be sat in the car outside a workplace that doesn't need me any more.
S2.fieldNote: Sam handles the shock like a bank adviser, going straight to the household budget. The image of sitting in the car outside a closed workplace recurs from his own past. He finds advising his son about debt painful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people take it seriously. I'd say government and firms should start the retraining now. I'd say it calmly, because panic never helped anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to get properly good and build up a list of Saturday customers. People will probably still want a person they trust in their house for a while, even if machines do the heavy work. In five years I could be the friendly face who turns up with the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the Saturday jobs going and grow them, maybe two days a month extra. I'd start using the AI more for quotes and planning once the crew does. And I'd keep saving hard, building to two years of bills instead of one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's time, but it's not that much time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change for you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes whether I'm the one being replaced or the one who knows the customers. With two years it all just stops. With five, I can build up a little name locally, and people buy from people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the friendly face with the robot'. Do you really believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half believe it. At the bank, the friendly faces lasted longest, but they did go in the end. I'd be buying time, not safety, and I know the difference.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people take it seriously, and retraining should start now. Panic never helped anybody.
S3.think: He thinks five years lets him get good and build up local customers who want someone they trust. He could be the friendly face who turns up with the robot.
S3.do: Grows his Saturday jobs by a couple of days a month and uses AI more for quotes once the crew does. Saves hard to build two years of bills instead of one.
S3.feel: Uneasy: there's time, but not much.
S3.quote: In five years I could be the friendly face who turns up with the robot.
S3.fieldNote: The extra years let Sam picture a role as the trusted local face. He's honest that it buys time rather than safety, a lesson from watching bank staff go in stages. His steady style shows in waiting for the crew before using more AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a sensible amount of time, and if we plan, most people can land on their feet. I'd say government should set out a clear plan, and firms should do their bit. Middle of the road, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years means a whole working stretch. I'd be 53, the mortgage would be nearly done, Oscar and Lily would be through school. Ten years from now, I'd rather be the man who plans the kitchen than the man who carries it in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years I'd finish learning the trade properly, then do a course in surveying or project management, the planning side of renovations. I'd put a bit more into my pension every month. And I'd sit down with the kids about subjects that'll last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a manageable way. It feels like a long project, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why surveying or project management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's where talking to customers and doing sums meet, and both are things I did at the bank. My knees won't love the tools at fifty anyway. The bank job I lost would turn out to be the bit of me that's still useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lily make of all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lily's eleven and wants to be a vet one week and a singer the next. I'd tell her to keep both. I'd tell her what I learned: things change slower than they say, but they do change.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a sensible amount of time and most people can land on their feet if we plan. Government should set out a clear plan and firms should do their bit.
S4.think: He sees ten years as a whole working stretch, with the mortgage nearly paid and the kids through school. He'd rather plan the kitchen than carry it in.
S4.do: Finishes learning the trade, then studies surveying or project management in the planning side of renovations. Pays a bit more into his pension monthly and talks to the kids about lasting subjects.
S4.feel: Uneasy but manageable, like a long project rather than a cliff.
S4.quote: The bank job I lost would turn out to be the bit of me that's still useful.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Sam plans to move from carrying kitchens to planning them, using his bank skills with numbers and customers. He finds it ironic that the job he lost becomes his asset. He remains careful and middle-of-the-road throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: That's all five. Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Mei and I would both be hit and there'd be no time to build anything. What would help is decent support while people retrain, and firms being honest early, not the day before. The bank told us three weeks before closing. Three weeks.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people still want from a person. The old ladies at the bank wanted someone to talk to, not just their money sorted. I think that's where the jobs will hang on longest, and nobody seems to plan for it.

headlineQuote: Ten years from now, I'd rather be the man who plans the kitchen than the man who carries it in.
portrait: Sam Chen is a 43-year-old junior on a family-run renovation crew, about three years in, after fifteen years in a bank branch that closed. His partner Mei is a pharmacist, and with his redundancy package they have a solid cushion and two children. He's a careful centrist who learns new tools once others prove them, and he reads every picture through the slow decline of bank branches. He's calm about the plateau and steady change, anxious about AGI in two years because both their jobs would go, and uneasy but planning with five or ten years, aiming to become the trusted local face or move into surveying.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he and Mei would both be hit with no time to build anything new.
whatWouldHelp: Decent support while people retrain, and firms being honest early rather than giving three weeks' notice like his bank did.
